learningObjective: Distinguish work-inefficient (Hillis-Steele) from work-efficient (Blelloch) parallel prefix-scan algorithms.
stem: Consider the two parallel inclusive-scan patterns below over a warp/block of N=32 threads. Which statement about the two algorithms is correct?

options.text: Hillis-Steele has depth O(log N) but does O(N log N) work; Blelloch has depth O(log N) and does O(N) work. Blelloch is 'work-efficient': asymptotically fewer operations, but its access pattern is more complex and often needs bank-conflict-avoiding padding on shared memory.
Both algorithms have identical work and depth; the choice between them is purely stylistic and yields identical performance on all NVIDIA architectures.
Hillis-Steele produces the correct output only when the reduction operator is commutative; Blelloch works for any operator. This is why Hillis-Steele is deprecated for FP addition (non-associative).
Blelloch has depth O(N/2) and work O(N); it is faster than Hillis-Steele on serial architectures but not on GPUs, where Hillis-Steele's O(N log N) work is preferred.

explanation: Hillis-Steele scan: at each of log N steps, thread `t` adds the value from `t - offset` — total work per element is O(log N), so total work is O(N log N). Blelloch (balanced tree) scan: up-sweep builds partial sums, down-sweep propagates prefixes; both phases have log N depth, but each thread participates in only a fraction of the tree — total work is O(N). On GPUs, Blelloch is 'work-efficient' (fewer ops), but its non-uniform access pattern requires care with shared-memory bank conflicts (padding trick). Hillis-Steele is simpler and can win in practice on small N due to its uniform access pattern.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: work vs depth trade-off; Blelloch is work-efficient but pattern-heavier.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: work costs differ (O(N log N) vs O(N)).
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: both require associativity; commutativity is not the differentiator.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: Blelloch depth is O(log N), not O(N).

assumptions: Both algorithms use shared memory with `__syncthreads()`.
N is a power of two.
nonImplications: Does not imply Blelloch is always faster on real GPU workloads.
Does not imply Hillis-Steele is incorrect for FP; it is correct but non-associative reductions have order-dependent results either way.

performanceClaim.scope: Asymptotic work/depth of parallel scan algorithms
